content: Skin-to-skin care (SSC), also known as kangaroo care (KC), is a non-pharmacological method used to manage pain in neonates. This technique involves direct contact between the infant and the caregiver's chest, mimicking the natural behavior of marsupials. The primary goal of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness of SSC in reducing pain during medical or nursing procedures in neonates, comparing it to no intervention, sucrose, other analgesics, or additional measures like rocking. The study also aimed to assess the impact of SSC duration, the person providing SSC, and its safety in relieving procedural pain. Additionally, the effects of SSC were analyzed across different postmenstrual age groups of infants. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL, up to February 2016. They also reviewed clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists for randomized and quasi-randomized trials. The studies included term infants (≥37 weeks postmenstrual age) and preterm infants (<37 weeks postmenstrual age) undergoing painful procedures while receiving SSC. The primary outcomes measured were physiological and behavioral pain indicators, as well as composite pain scores. A total of 25 studies involving 2001 infants were included. Among these, 19 studies focused on heel lance as the painful procedure, while others examined venepuncture, intramuscular injections, vaccinations, and tape removal. The studies were generally of high quality, though blinding of the intervention was not feasible, introducing potential bias in outcome scoring. Seventeen studies compared SSC to no treatment. Heart rate data from five studies (161 infants) showed a significant reduction in heart rate during painful procedures with SSC (mean difference [MD] −10.78 beats per minute, 95% confidence interval [CI] −13.63 to −7.93). However, four studies (120 infants) found no difference in heart rate after the procedure. Two studies reported no significant differences in heart rate variability. Similarly, two studies analyzing oxygen saturation at 30 and 60 seconds post-procedure found no differences. Crying duration was significantly reduced with SSC in four studies (133 infants), with a greater reduction observed during heel lance (MD −34.16 seconds, 95% CI −42.86 to −25.45) compared to intramuscular injections (MD −8.83 seconds, 95% CI −14.63 to −3.02). The Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP) was used as a primary outcome in five studies (267 infants). SSC significantly reduced PIPP scores at 30 seconds (MD −3.21, 95% CI −3.94 to −2.47), 60 seconds (MD −1.64, 95% CI −2.86 to −0.43), and 90 seconds (MD −1.28, 95% CI −2.53 to −0.04) post-procedure. However, no difference was observed at 120 seconds (MD 0.07, 95% CI −1.11 to 1.25). Data on heart rate returning to baseline, cortisol levels, and facial actions were insufficient for meta-analysis. Eight studies compared SSC to other interventions, with or without a no-treatment control. Two crossover studies (80 infants) found no significant differences in PIPP scores when SSC was provided by the mother versus another caregiver (e.g., father or another female). One study (640 infants) found that SSC combined with dextrose was most effective, followed by SSC alone, which was more effective than dextrose alone. Another study (95 infants) showed SSC was more effective than oral glucose in reducing heart rate. SSC, either alone or combined with breastfeeding, was superior to no treatment but not significantly different from breastfeeding alone. One study (127 infants) found that combining SSC with sucrose and breastfeeding was more effective than SSC alone in reducing crying time and NIPS scores. Another study (50 infants) found SSC and expressed breast milk equally effective in reducing PIPP scores. There was insufficient data to compare the effects of SSC across different age groups or durations of SSC. No adverse events were reported in any of the studies. In conclusion, SSC appears to be effective in reducing pain during single painful procedures in neonates, as evidenced by composite pain indicators, heart rate, and crying time. Behavioral indicators generally favored SSC, though facial actions were more prone to observer bias. Physiological indicators showed mixed results, with heart rate consistently favoring SSC. Studies comparing maternal providers to other caregivers showed no significant differences. There was considerable variability in studies with behavioral or composite outcomes. Further research is needed to determine the optimal duration of SSC, its effects across gestational age groups, its repeated use, and its long-term effects. Additionally, the potential synergistic effects of SSC combined with other interventions warrant further investigation.
